They opened the robotics club again. You are going this time, right?
I do not know. Two years ago it was on the same afternoon as football, and I chose football.
Everyone chose football. Nobody wanted to be the only one in a lab.
Exactly. And if I had joined the club then, I would be building things every weekend now instead of watching other people do it.
So you regret playing football. That is a trade-off, not a disaster.
I do not regret football. I regret the reason. If I were less afraid of being the odd one out, I would not have decided it in ten seconds.
Did anybody try to talk you out of it?
My brother did. He asked whether I could do both, and I never even checked. So I paid for it in the long run, and the thing at stake was smaller than I thought.
Then this is your second chance at the same choice. That is the only kind that counts.
If I had chosen differently, I would be somewhere else today.

Hi Mark. In lesson fourteen you learned the third conditional, where a different past gives you a different past. If I had studied, I would have passed. Both halves live in the past, and the sentence stays there. Today we break that symmetry, because real life is not symmetrical. A mixed conditional puts the two halves in different times. The first shape is the common one. The condition is in the past and the result is now. If I had taken that job, I would be living in another city today. Notice the form. If plus had plus the past participle in the first half, and would plus the bare verb in the second half. No have, no been. The second shape runs the other way. The condition is something permanent about you, and the result sits in the past. If I were more patient, I would not have said that. Here the first half is if plus the past simple, and the second half is would have plus the past participle. Both shapes exist because a decision has two lives. One is the moment you made it, and the other is the person you are because of it. Before class, think of one choice that still shapes your week, and try to say it both ways. See you on Friday, Mark.

There is one decision I keep coming back to, and it was not even a big one at the time. Two years ago my school offered a robotics club and a football team on the same afternoon, and I had about a week to choose. I chose football, because my friends were going, and because I did not want to be the only one sitting in a lab. Now, if I had joined the robotics club, I would probably be building things every weekend instead of watching other people build them online. That is the part that annoys me. The strange thing is that I do not regret playing football. I regret the reason. If I were less afraid of being the odd one out, I would not have decided it in ten seconds, and I would have asked whether I could do both. Nobody told me that was possible, and I never asked. So the trade-off was real, but it was smaller than I thought, and I paid for it in the long run. This year the club opened again. I am not going to be impulsive about it twice.

First, you name the decision itself, in the past simple, so we know what actually happened. Then you say what was at stake, so we understand why the choice was difficult. After that, you build the first mixed conditional: if plus had plus the past participle for the condition, and would plus the bare verb for the result you would be living today. Next, you turn it around with the second shape, using if plus the past simple for the thing that is permanently true about you, and would have plus the past participle for what you would have done differently. Finally, you say what you would do now, because the point of analysing a decision is the next one, not the old one.
